name: Hana Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up, make tea, and check whether any ad agencies have sent jingle briefs overnight. If they have, I record in a booth I built in my wardrobe with foam and a duvet. Afternoons and evenings I teach singing over video, about twenty students a week, and once a month I have a residency at a wine bar, two sets of my own songs and covers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I use AI to make backing tracks for students in their key, to turn lessons into practice notes, and to sort my calendar. I post covers online too, about four thousand followers, which brings in students but not much money. I live alone in a studio flat, and my older sister lives ten minutes away, which has saved me more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: the tools are great helpers, and people still want a real voice. I'd probably make a little video about how I use AI in lessons, because my students ask. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the small stuff already bites. A cheap advert can use a generated voice now, and my jingle rate's gone from two hundred to about a hundred in a year. Even if AI never gets any smarter, cheap AI voices have already halved what an ad agency will pay me to sing ten seconds about yoghurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the teaching, because that's growing: I'd add a group class on Sunday evenings for six students at fifteen each. I'd keep using the AI tools to save time on backing tracks and notes. And I'd pitch to two more agencies for jingle work, while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, honestly. I like my life, but the money is held together with tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does "held together with tape" look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine hundred in savings, which is three weeks. In August two agencies paid late at the same time and I had to borrow rent from my sister. She didn't mind, but I minded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for jingle rates falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, or everyone. Agencies are squeezed by clients, and clients are squeezed by prices. I don't think there's a villain, just a lot of people looking for a cheaper option, me included when I buy things.

I'd make a short **video** about how I use AI in lessons.
think: Cheap **AI voices** have already cut my jingle rate roughly in half.
My money is **held together with tape**, even in a quiet world.
do: Add a Sunday **group class** for six students at fifteen each.
Keep using **AI tools** for backing tracks and practice notes.
Pitch to **two more agencies** for jingle work.
feel: A bit **anxious**, liking her life but not her **finances**.

fieldNote: Even in AI Plateau, **AI voices** have already cut her jingle income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say singers need to own their voices, and there should be clear rules about cloning someone's voice without paying. I'd share how I'm adapting, because I think people want practical stuff, not doom. I'd also say I'm not anti-AI; I use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the jingle work is gone within a year or two, and that's forty percent of my income. Online lessons get squeezed too, because an AI vocal coach app is cheaper than me. I use AI every day, and I'm still about to watch a computer take forty percent of my income from my wardrobe booth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into licensing my own voice to one of the AI voice companies, properly, with a contract and a fee each time it's used. I'd move my teaching towards in-person lessons and choirs, because that's harder to copy. And I'd start a community choir at the library on Thursday nights, with a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but curious too. I can see doors closing and some new ones opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Licensing your voice sounds like helping the thing that replaces you. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Conflicted, honestly. But if my voice is going to be copied anyway, I'd rather be paid for it and have a say in how it's used. A friend of mine signed with one of those companies last year and gets a small monthly cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My new microphone fund, then the yearly songwriting retreat, which is three hundred. I'd also cancel two of the software subscriptions I barely use. Rent and my sister's birthday present stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for everyone, quickly, not just for musicians, because this is everybody's problem. I'd post about practical things, like how to keep earning in person while there's time. I'd try not to add to the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, everything I do on a screen is gone by 2028: jingles, online lessons, even my covers channel, because there'll be endless free AI covers. What's left is my body in a room, singing or teaching, until around 2031. My whole career is on a screen, so AGI by 2028 means I have two years to become someone who only works in rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd build in-person work: the choir, singing lessons at two schools if they'd take me, and singing at weddings and funerals, which need a human. I'd sell the recording gear I won't need, maybe eight hundred. And I'd ask my sister whether I could move into her spare room to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but moving. I'm better when I'm doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come around 2031, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe people will still want a real person singing at their mum's funeral, even if a robot could. That's the bet I'd be making, and I know it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your students, the ones learning to sing for a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to sing because they love it, and to learn something hands-on as well. That's hard advice to give a nineteen-year-old who wants to be famous. I'd give it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain, so governments should pay for it now, not in 2030. I'd post my own plan. I'd also say voice cloning rules need to be sorted before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is workable for me. The jingles go early anyway, but I'd have time to build the in-person side properly. Five years is enough time for me to swap a wardrobe booth for a choir of forty people who need me there every Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the community choir this year and aim to grow it to forty people at five each a week. I'd do a part-time qualification in choir leading, about five hundred, and use AI to handle the admin and arrangements. I'd try to save a hundred a month from the choir money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. Like a big move you've chosen, not one done to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Forty people in a choir. Is that realistic where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's one choir in town already, and it has a waiting list. So yes, I think so, if I make it friendly and cheap. Half of it is tea and biscuits, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still license your voice in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, early on, while it pays. I'd stop if the contract let them use my voice for anything I'd hate, like political adverts. That's the small print I'd actually read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a real chance to get this right: training money, voice rights, support for people who lose work. I'd be one of the calm voices online, sharing what's working. And I'd say live music is worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, with time to build something solid. The jingles still go early, before full AGI, so the next few years are the hard bit. With ten years, my worry isn't the robots in 2039, it's paying rent in 2027 while the jingle money dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the choir and in-person teaching steadily, and maybe start a second choir for older people at a care home. I'd do the choir-leading qualification next year. I'd also open a pension, finally, even at twenty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, mostly. A bit restless, because a decade feels long enough to make a big mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What big mistake are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Signing a voice deal that lets a company use me forever for a few hundred. Or putting everything into the online channel, then watching it drown in free AI covers. I'd want to spread my bets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about moving to a bigger city for more gigs. With ten years, I'd probably do it in three or four years, once the choir's running and I could hand it over. With two, I'd stay near my sister.

**Live music** is worth paying for, and I'd keep saying so.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because all my work is on a screen and two years isn't enough to rebuild it in person. What would help is clear rules on voice cloning, so I'm paid when my voice is used, and cheap training for things like choir leading.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd miss. A generated voice can hit every note, but it has never been nervous before a funeral and sung anyway.

headlineQuote: A generated voice can hit every note, but it has never been nervous before a funeral and sung anyway.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old singer** who records jingles in a wardrobe booth and teaches online.

She uses **AI daily** and sees no villain, just everyone chasing cheaper options.
Her plan is to trade **screen work** for in-person choirs, and to license her voice.
The fast scenario frightens her most because her whole career sits **on a screen**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to rebuild in person.
whatWouldHelp: **Voice cloning rules** that pay singers when their voice is used.
